claims.text: The studied system is an as-deposited RF magnetron-sputtered Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer coating with a controlled lamellar microstructure.
Reducing individual layer thickness increases interface density in Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer coatings.
Increasing interface density enhances resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Interfaces in the multilayer coating act as barriers to dislocation propagation.
Thinner layers reduce dislocation mobility during time-dependent plastic deformation relative to thicker layers.
Coatings with thinner individual layers will have significantly lower nanoindentation creep rates than coatings with thicker layers.
Thicker-layer Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayers have fewer effective barriers to dislocation motion.
Thicker-layer Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayers are expected to have higher creep rates than thinner-layer multilayers.
The layer-thickness effect is expected to be significant when individual layers are below roughly 100 nm.
Outside the stated thickness regime, interface effects may be diminished or altered by intermixing or other deposition parameters.
Interface coherency and interdiffusion can alter the efficiency of interfaces as barriers to dislocation movement.
Individual layer thickness should be varied systematically while nanoindentation load and temperature are held constant.
Electron microscopy should be used to assess interface quality and density across the layer-thickness series.
Failure of thinner layers to produce consistently lower creep rates than thicker layers would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe an increase in effective interface-barrier density, including because of interdiffusion, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
